title: Long-term survival (≥2 years) in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis: a systematic review of prolonged survivors.

analysis.scope_and_question: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a progressive and often fatal disorder with highly variable survival. This systematic review aimed to characterize long-term survival (≥2 years), remission, and stabilization, and identify determinants of favorable outcomes.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies including confirmed SSPE cases were considered eligible for inclusion. Individual patient analysis was restricted to cases with ≥2 years of follow-up. Data were extracted at the patient and cohort levels.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Analysis of 77 patients demonstrated that survival beyond 2 years is achievable but variable. Survival distribution showed 44.2% surviving 2 to <5 years, 28.6% surviving 5 to <10 years, and 27.3% surviving ≥10 years. Although 62.3% initially achieved remission or stabilization, 31.2% later developed progression, severe disability, or death. Reported factors associated with prolonged survival included treatment responsiveness (62.3%), slow disease progression (24.7%), and relapsing-remitting or biphasic patterns (20.8%). Additional contributors were host-related factors (18.2%), adult-onset disease (10.4%), early diagnosis, and electroencephalographic improvement. Across 31 cohort studies, overall survival remained poor.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Survival beyond 2 years was inconsistently reported and varied widely. Remission or stabilization was observed in some studies, but disease progression remained the predominant outcome. Mortality ranged from low to very high across cohorts. Reported factors associated with improved survival included slower disease progression, older age at onset, earlier stage at diagnosis, and use of therapies such as inosine pranobex and interferon.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Although prolonged survival occurs in some, most patients have poor outcomes, emphasizing the importance of early diagnosis and the need for effective therapies.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review examines long-term survival (≥2 years) in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a progressive and often fatal disorder. Analyzing 77 patients and 31 cohort studies, the review finds marked heterogeneity in survival outcomes, with 44.2% surviving 2-5 years, 28.6% surviving 5-10 years, and 27.3% surviving ≥10 years. While 62.3% initially achieved remission or stabilization, 31.2% later progressed to severe disability or death. Factors associated with prolonged survival included treatment responsiveness, slow disease progression, relapsing-remitting patterns, host-related factors, adult-onset disease, early diagnosis, and EEG improvement. Despite some cases of prolonged survival, most patients have poor outcomes, highlighting the need for early diagnosis and effective therapies.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study assessed measles immunity seroprevalence among 175 healthcare workers in Bandar Abbas following the 2025 outbreak. Despite all participants reporting prior vaccination, 25.1% lacked positive immunity, with younger staff showing significantly lower immunity levels. Age was a significant predictor of immunity status, increasing odds by 14.3% per year, while sex showed no association. The findings highlight concerning immunity gaps among HCWs, particularly in younger cohorts, necessitating targeted screening, booster vaccinations, and enhanced infection control measures to prevent nosocomial transmission during outbreaks.

title: From Seroprevalence to Measles Outbreak Risk: A Multicountry Epidemiological Proof of Concept

analysis.research_question_and_background: High national vaccination coverage may conceal age-specific and spatially concentrated measles susceptibility. The study aimed to assess whether published age-specific seropositivity results can be converted into a time-updated susceptibility profile that corresponds with subsequent measles incidence.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a multicountry epidemiological proof of concept using published seropositivity data from Israel, the Netherlands, Czechia, and Australia. For Israel, 2015 age-specific seropositivity estimates were mapped to monthly birth cohorts and projected to 1 March 2018.
analysis.methods: Published seropositivity estimates were mapped to monthly birth cohorts and projected over time, accounting for births, aging, maternal antibody, routine vaccination, vaccine effectiveness, and assay uncertainty. External comparisons used a common framework covering age distribution, assay classification, vaccination, importation, spatial concentration, and transmission context.
analysis.main_results: The estimated number susceptible in Israel on 1 March 2018 ranged from 0.55 million (6.3%) to 1.92 million (22.4%), with a central estimate of 1.22 million (14.2%). Children aged <1 year had the highest central susceptible proportion (75.7%) and incidence (196.0 per 100,000). Jerusalem District accounted for 2,202 of 4,311 national cases, with susceptibility concentrated in communities with lower first-dose coverage.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Published seropositivity can identify immunity gaps, but useful outbreak-risk assessment must also represent susceptible density, introduction pressure, and local transmission conditions. The model identified substantial susceptibility during early childhood, supporting Israel's decision to advance the second MMRV dose from 6 years to 18 months.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform targeted vaccination strategies by highlighting age-specific susceptibility hotspots and the importance of spatial coverage. They demonstrate that seroprevalence data, when properly modeled, can predict outbreak risk and guide policy adjustments to reduce transmission windows in high-risk groups.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The model was not designed to directly compare alternative vaccination schedules, and external comparisons were limited by varying data quality and outbreak contexts. The evidence strength is moderate, as the approach is biologically plausible and validated against observed outbreaks, but relies on assumptions about vaccine effectiveness and assay accuracy.

analysis.summary_en: This multicountry study developed a method to convert seroprevalence data into time-updated measles susceptibility profiles, validated against the 2018-2019 Israeli outbreak. The model estimated 0.55-1.92 million susceptible individuals in Israel (6.3-22.4%), with highest risk in infants (<1 year, 75.7% susceptible, 196/100,000 incidence). Jerusalem District accounted for 51% of cases, reflecting spatial clustering in low-coverage communities. External comparisons showed outbreak risk amplification in the Netherlands due to clustering, survey design effects in Czechia, and importation dominance in Australia. The approach identified early childhood susceptibility gaps, supporting Israel's policy to advance the second MMRV dose from 6 years to 18 months. The study demonstrates that seroprevalence data, when combined with demographic and vaccination dynamics, can predict outbreak risk and guide targeted interventions, though accuracy depends on local transmission conditions and data quality.

title: Addressing the Measles Epidemic: Evidence Informed Approaches Schools Can Use to Promote Childhood Vaccination.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the re-emergence of measles as an epidemic threat in the United States, despite its elimination in 2000, and examines the role of schools in promoting childhood vaccination amid declining vaccination rates and policy changes.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a narrative review focusing on the resurgence of measles in the United States from January 2025 to April 2026, with a particular emphasis on school-aged children and the impact of federal policy shifts.
analysis.methods: The analysis is based on a review of reported measles cases, federal court decisions, and policy changes, without generating or analyzing new datasets.
analysis.main_results: From January 2025 to April 2026, there were 4,102 diagnosed measles cases in the United States, with 92.5% of cases being unvaccinated or having unknown vaccination status; 23.7% of cases were in children under 5 years, and 47.4% in those aged 5–19.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the resurgence as a consequence of declining vaccination rates, politicization of immunization policy, and erosion of institutional authority, with federal policy shifts exacerbating the epidemic.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for schools to implement evidence-informed strategies to promote vaccination, protect vulnerable students, manage outbreaks, and counter misinformation in polarized environments.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate, as the study relies on reported cases and policy analyses without primary data collection or controlled experiments, and the narrative review approach may introduce bias.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the re-emergence of measles in the United States, which was declared eliminated in 2000 but has resurged as an epidemic threat. From January 2025 to April 2026, 4,102 cases were reported, with 92.5% unvaccinated or of unknown status, disproportionately affecting children under 5 (23.7%) and those aged 5–19 (47.4%). The resurgence is attributed to declining vaccination rates, politicization of immunization policy, and federal policy shifts, including attempts to reduce recommended childhood vaccines and cut infectious disease prevention funding. Federal courts have intervened to block these changes, citing their potential to harm public health. Schools, now at the epicenter of the outbreak, face challenges in protecting vulnerable students, managing exclusion policies, and countering misinformation. The study underscores the need for evidence-informed strategies to promote vaccination and maintain public trust.

title: Changing epidemiology and transmission dynamics of measles in Ho Chi Minh City: a comparison of the 2018–2020 and 2024–2025 outbreaks

analysis.research_question_and_background: Measles remains a major public health threat worldwide. The study aimed to understand the changing epidemiology and transmission dynamics of measles in Ho Chi Minh City.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study compared measles outbreaks in Ho Chi Minh City during 2018–2020 and 2024–2025. Line-list data for measles cases were extracted from the infectious disease surveillance system between 2018 and 2025.
analysis.methods: Demographic changes were assessed using cross-sectional age distributions and longitudinal birth-cohort analyses. Transmission dynamics were characterized by estimating the effective reproduction number (Rt) using the Cori and Wallinga–Teunis methods.
analysis.main_results: The 2018–2020 outbreak primarily affected children under five years of age (median age 3.75 years, IQR 0.9–9.1), whereas the 2024–2025 outbreak shifted toward older age groups (median age 8.4 years, IQR 1–14). The 2024–2025 outbreak also showed broader spatial spread and a reversed geographic trajectory compared with the earlier epidemic.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings suggest that age-restricted outbreak response immunization may leave residual susceptible populations that contribute to future outbreaks. Transmission patterns changed substantially, with the 2018–2020 outbreak sustained mainly by transmission among young children, whereas the 2024–2025 outbreak was driven by older age groups, with individuals >15 years acting as an important source of infection for infants.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Achieving sustainable measles elimination will require vaccination strategies that address historical immunity gaps across all vulnerable age groups, in addition to maintaining high routine childhood vaccination coverage.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific limitations of the study design.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the changing epidemiology and transmission dynamics of measles in Ho Chi Minh City, comparing the 2018–2020 and 2024–2025 outbreaks. It highlights a shift from primarily affecting young children to involving older age groups, particularly those over 15 years, who became important sources of infection for infants. The study used line-list data from the infectious disease surveillance system and analyzed demographic changes through cross-sectional age distributions and longitudinal birth-cohort analyses. It also estimated the effective reproduction number (Rt) using the Cori and Wallinga–Teunis methods. The findings suggest that age-restricted immunization campaigns may leave susceptible populations that contribute to future outbreaks, emphasizing the need for vaccination strategies that address immunity gaps across all vulnerable age groups. The study provides important insights for public health planning and surveillance, but it does not report specific limitations of the study design.

title: Risk-targeted interventions for measles control-Lessons from an emergency response project in the Katanga Region, Democratic Republic of the Congo (2021-2023)

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study was needed to address operational challenges in measles control in the Katanga region of the Democratic Republic of Congo, where recurrent epidemics have substantial public health impact, and it aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a risk-targeted approach for measles prevention and control.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted in the Katanga region of the Democratic Republic of Congo from 2021 to 2023, focusing on selected high-risk health zones, and evaluated the Urgepi project's risk-targeted approach using surveillance data.
analysis.methods: The study evaluated targeted preventive activities, explored strategies for prioritizing interventions amid multiple alerts, and assessed the impact of interventions on measles epidemics using surveillance data from 2021-2023.
analysis.main_results: Preventive vaccination averted epidemics in six of nine vaccinated high-risk health zones, while nine of ten non-vaccinated priority health zones experienced large epidemics; the Urgepi alert prioritization score was positively associated with subsequent epidemic size; and a 50% reduction in median epidemic duration was recorded.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as demonstrating the effectiveness of the risk-targeted approach for measles prevention and control, highlighting the importance of timely and context-specific interventions, and demonstrated how such an approach can optimize resources in the fight against measles.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform national programs on how to prioritize geographic areas for measles prevention and outbreak response when operational constraints make it infeasible to cover all regions, and demonstrate the value of risk-targeted approaches in optimizing resource allocation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate, as no clear impact of epidemic response vaccination on case numbers was observed, likely due to biases introduced in case reporting through provision of free case management, and the study's effectiveness is limited to the specific context of the Katanga region.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the Urgepi project's risk-targeted approach for measles control in the Katanga region of the Democratic Republic of Congo from 2021-2023. The project directed resources to selected high-risk health zones to strengthen surveillance, implement preventive vaccination, and ensure timely epidemic response. Findings show that preventive vaccination successfully averted epidemics in six of nine vaccinated high-risk health zones, while nine of ten non-vaccinated priority health zones experienced large epidemics. The alert prioritization score was positively associated with subsequent epidemic size, and a 50% reduction in median epidemic duration was recorded. Although no clear impact of epidemic response vaccination on case numbers was observed, likely due to reporting biases, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of risk-targeted approaches for measles prevention and control, highlighting the importance of timely and context-specific interventions.

title: Investigating the Trifecta of Measles Cases, Vaccination Rates, and Homeschooling in the United States

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study was needed due to the resurgence in measles cases in the United States, which has sparked concern about increased hospitalizations and mortality rates despite the availability of a well-tolerated and effective vaccine.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A study was conducted to assess the effect of homeschooling and vaccination rates on measles cases in the United States.
analysis.methods: The study employed statistical tests, multiple regression, and Pearson correlation coefficient to analyze the relationship between MMR average vaccination rates from 2015 to 2025, homeschooling data from 2024, and measles cases.
analysis.main_results: Regression analysis revealed homeschooling had a significant effect on the number of measles cases (P=.004) with a positive correlation (r=0.4, P=0.01), while the vaccination rate variable was not statistically significant, though the correlation coefficient was positive (r=0.06, P>0.05).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret these findings as adding to the current body of knowledge as researchers continue to explore causes for the recent spike in measles cases in the United States.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that homeschooling may be a contributing factor to the resurgence of measles cases, highlighting the need for further investigation into non-vaccination-related factors in disease transmission.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate, as the study identifies a significant correlation between homeschooling and measles cases but does not establish causation, and the vaccination rate variable was not statistically significant.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the resurgence of measles cases in the United States, focusing on the potential impact of homeschooling and vaccination rates. Using statistical methods including multiple regression and Pearson correlation, the research found a significant positive correlation between homeschooling and measles cases (r=0.4, P=0.01), while vaccination rates showed no statistical significance despite a positive correlation (r=0.06, P>0.05). The findings contribute to understanding non-vaccination factors in measles transmission, suggesting homeschooling may play a role in disease resurgence, though causation cannot be established from this analysis.

title: Measles and Rubella Elimination Trends in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region, 2023–2024: Progress and Recent Epidemiological Shifts

analysis.research_question_and_background: Measles and rubella remain key indicators of immunization system performance and are central to the Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030). Disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic have widened immunity gaps and accelerated resurgence of vaccine-preventable diseases across multiple regions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study assesses progress toward measles and rubella elimination in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR) during 2023–2024. Key indicators included disease incidence, MCV1 and MCV2 coverage, surveillance performance metrics, and verified elimination status.
analysis.methods: We conducted a retrospective descriptive analysis of measles and rubella surveillance data, WHO/UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC), and Joint Reporting Form (eJRF) data for all 22 EMR countries and territories.
analysis.main_results: Regional measles incidence increased from 110.8 to 116.3 per million population, while rubella incidence more than doubled from 1.9 to 4.3 per million. Large outbreaks in Yemen, Iraq, and Afghanistan disproportionally drove regional trends. MCV1 coverage remained stable at approximately 80%, while MCV2 coverage increased marginally from 73% to 75%. Only nine of 22 countries achieved ≥95% coverage for both doses in 2024. Persistent zero-dose populations, high dropout rates, and ongoing immunity gaps sustained transmission across multiple settings.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The EMR remains off track to achieve measles and rubella elimination by 2030. Accelerated, equity-focused efforts are urgently needed to strengthen routine immunization systems, reduce zero-dose population, enhance surveillance capacity, and improve outbreak response—particularly in fragile and conflicted-affected settings.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for targeted interventions to address immunity gaps and strengthen immunization systems in the EMR, particularly in countries experiencing outbreaks and low vaccination coverage.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on retrospective data and does not account for real-time changes in immunization practices or outbreak dynamics. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the reliance on reported data rather than direct observation or experimental validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates progress toward measles and rubella elimination in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR) during 2023–2024. It highlights that measles incidence increased slightly, while rubella incidence more than doubled, with large outbreaks in Yemen, Iraq, and Afghanistan driving regional trends. Despite stable MCV1 coverage and a marginal increase in MCV2 coverage, only nine countries achieved ≥95% coverage for both doses. Persistent zero-dose populations and immunity gaps continue to sustain transmission. The authors conclude that the EMR remains off track to meet elimination targets by 2030 and emphasize the need for accelerated, equity-focused efforts to strengthen immunization systems and outbreak response, particularly in fragile settings. The evidence is moderate in strength due to its reliance on reported data rather than direct observation.

title: Investigation of measles outbreak in Pakistan (2022 to 2023): Exploring comorbidities, complications, and molecular characterization

analysis.research_question_and_background: Measles remains a major public health concern worldwide, particularly in regions with insufficient vaccination coverage and healthcare infrastructure, like Pakistan.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The purpose of this study is to investigate the epidemiological, molecular, and phylogenetic characteristics of the measles outbreak in Pakistan during 2022-2023 and highlight the areas of improvement that can contribute to the better understanding of the disease and inform strategies for effective outbreak management and vaccination optimization.
analysis.methods: Throat swabs were collected from patients (n = 183) admitted at PIMS, Islamabad, Pakistan, from December 2022- December 2023. Statistical analysis of data was conducted on SPSS-21 software.
analysis.main_results: Most of the measles patients were infants with a high prevalence of comorbidity and complications, and significant number of patients had inadequate vaccination coverage. The phylogenetic analysis revealed relatedness to B3 strains circulating in Russia and the USA, emphasizing the global spread. The amino acid substitutions and structure analysis highlighted minor structural variations in current isolates as compared to the reference strain.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings underscore the importance of continuous surveillance and understanding of measles epidemiology and viral variations for effective outbreak management and vaccination optimization.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for improved vaccination strategies and surveillance systems to mitigate the morbidity and mortality associated with measles outbreaks in Pakistan and similar settings globally.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the measles outbreak in Pakistan from 2022 to 2023, focusing on epidemiological, molecular, and phylogenetic characteristics. It highlights the high prevalence of comorbidities and complications among infants, along with inadequate vaccination coverage. The phylogenetic analysis shows relatedness to B3 strains in Russia and the USA, indicating global spread, while structural variations in isolates compared to the reference strain are noted. The study emphasizes the importance of continuous surveillance and understanding of measles epidemiology and viral variations for effective outbreak management and vaccination optimization. The findings suggest the need for improved vaccination strategies and surveillance systems to address the public health challenges posed by measles outbreaks in Pakistan and similar regions. The evidence is strong, with no reported limitations.

title: Seroprevalence of measles-specific IgM and IgG antibodies among children (0–12 years) with measles-like symptoms: a hospital-based cross-sectional study in Northeast Nigeria

analysis.research_question_and_background: Nigeria has one of the highest measles burdens and the lowest vaccination coverage worldwide, and despite efforts to eliminate measles by 2030, outbreaks persist due to conflicts and the COVID-19 pandemic.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Children with clinically suspected measles cases were recruited from selected primary healthcare centres in Yobe, Borno and Adamawa between November 2022-July 2023, with serum samples analysed for measles-specific IgM (n=558) and IgG (n=372) antibodies.
analysis.methods: IgM antibodies were determined using the EUROIMMUN measles virus IgM ELISA kit, and IgG antibodies were determined using the Calbiotech measles IgG kit, with odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals calculated using univariate logistic regression.
analysis.main_results: The seroprevalence was 29.2% for measles IgM and 32.8% for measles IgG, with higher detection in males (30.6% and 33.3%) and children aged 1–3 years (40.8% and 46.5%), while vaccination significantly reduced infection odds (OR 0.30; 95% CI, 0.20–0.44; P ≤ 0.005).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study confirms a high frequency of measles seropositivity among symptomatic children in Northeast Nigeria, highlighting the need for localised investigation into immunization history in symptomatic cases.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings emphasize the importance of improving vaccination coverage and surveillance to reduce measles transmission in conflict-affected regions with disrupted health infrastructure.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by potential selection and recall biases, and its focus on symptomatic children reduces generalisability, with evidence strength assessed as moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This hospital-based cross-sectional study in Northeast Nigeria evaluated seroprevalence of measles-specific IgM and IgG antibodies among children with measles-like symptoms. Recruited from primary healthcare centres in Yobe, Borno, and Adamawa between November 2022 and July 2023, the study analysed 558 serum samples for IgM and 372 for IgG using ELISA kits. Results showed a seroprevalence of 29.2% for IgM and 32.8% for IgG, with higher detection in males and children aged 1–3 years. Vaccination significantly reduced infection odds (OR 0.30; 95% CI, 0.20–0.44; P ≤ 0.005). The study highlights high measles seropositivity in symptomatic children, emphasizing the need for improved vaccination coverage and surveillance in conflict-affected regions. Limitations include selection and recall biases, with moderate evidence strength due to these constraints.

title: Evaluation of measles and acute flaccid paralysis surveillance systems in Southern Province, Zambia, 2022 - 2024

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study evaluated measles and acute flaccid paralysis surveillance systems in Southern Province, Zambia, to assess their performance and identify gaps in data quality and operational challenges.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional surveillance system evaluation was conducted in Southern Province, Zambia, from 2022 to 2024, purposively selecting three districts and three facilities from each district based on measles and AFP case burden and vaccination coverage.
analysis.methods: Data on system simplicity, usefulness, and acceptability were collected from 27 participants using structured questionnaires, while data completeness, timeliness, and accuracy were assessed from the electronic Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (eIDSR) system and WHO databases.
analysis.main_results: The surveillance systems demonstrated high simplicity (84.6%), usefulness (90.5%), and acceptability (90.8%), but suboptimal data quality with mean completeness of 66.7%, timeliness of 51.1%, and accuracy of 50%, alongside operational challenges like inadequate specimen transport and insufficient funding.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors concluded that while the systems are functional and well-integrated, significant gaps in data quality limit their effectiveness for early outbreak detection and timely public health response.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Strengthening data management, specimen transport, and sustainable financing is critical to improving surveillance performance and advancing vaccine-preventable disease control and elimination targets in Zambia.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate due to suboptimal data quality and operational challenges, though the evaluation followed CDC guidelines and included multiple data sources.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated measles and acute flaccid paralysis surveillance systems in Southern Province, Zambia, from 2022 to 2024. Using a cross-sectional design following CDC guidelines, researchers assessed three districts and facilities, collecting data from 27 participants and electronic systems. The systems showed high simplicity (84.6%), usefulness (90.5%), and acceptability (90.8%), but suffered from suboptimal data quality (66.7% completeness, 51.1% timeliness, 50% accuracy) and operational challenges like inadequate specimen transport and funding. The authors concluded that while functional, the systems' effectiveness for early outbreak detection is limited by data gaps, emphasizing the need for improved data management, transport, and financing to meet disease control targets.

title: Preliminary safety data from a randomised trial of early versus standard timing of administration of measles-rubella vaccine in Ugandan infants

analysis.research_question_and_background: Measles remains a major cause of child morbidity and mortality in low-resource settings, and young infants are particularly at risk of severe disease, with many lacking protective levels of maternal antibodies by six months.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted an open-label randomised controlled non-inferiority trial at four health facilities in Kampala, Uganda, where infants aged 24–28 weeks were randomly assigned to receive MR at six and 12 months (group A), nine and 18 months (group B) or six and 18 months (group C).
analysis.methods: Infants were electronically randomised in a 1:1:1 ratio using block randomisation of varying sizes, stratified by site, maternal HIV status and baseline haemoglobin level, and caretakers recorded solicited reactions on paper diary cards, with safety-related events evaluated.
analysis.main_results: 450 infants received MR1 and were enrolled; no differences in local or systemic post-vaccination events between the six and nine months MR1 groups were observed [Local: 21·2% versus 21·9% (p = 0·959), systemic: 29·2% vs. 27·7% (p = 0·845)], and most local reactions were mild and within the first four days.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: We provide further evidence on the safety of administering a measles-containing vaccine at six months of age, addressing concerns about its effectiveness at this age.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support earlier vaccination in high-burden settings to potentially confer earlier protection, with no increased safety risks observed.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate due to the preliminary nature of the findings and the open-label design, which may introduce bias, though the randomisation and stratification enhance reliability.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents preliminary safety data from a randomised trial in Ugandan infants comparing early (six months) versus standard (nine months) measles-rubella vaccination. The trial enrolled 450 infants, randomised into three groups, and found no significant differences in local or systemic post-vaccination events between the six and nine months groups. Most reactions were mild and short-lived, with one non-vaccine-related death reported. The study provides evidence supporting the safety of early measles vaccination, potentially offering earlier protection in high-burden settings, though further data on effectiveness is needed.

title: Distinct Humoral Response Development to Measles Virus across Vaccine Platforms 2251461

analysis.research_question_and_background: As measles incidences increase globally, it is imperative to elucidate the features of a protective humoral response.
analysis.study_design_and_population: In this study, rhesus macaques were infected with wild-type measles virus or vaccinated with a live-attenuated measles vaccine, the triple measles mumps rubella vaccine, or a novel recombinant measles hemagglutinin protein-based vaccine.
analysis.methods: Phage-display immunoprecipitation sequencing technology (VirScan) was employed to evaluate viral epitope coverage by antibodies, and vaccinated animals were challenged with wild-type measles virus to measure antibody epitope reactivity during a recall.
analysis.main_results: Wild-type measles virus infection elicited antibodies with a broader epitope reactivity profile than live-attenuated vaccine-containing vaccines, and the recombinant measles hemagglutinin protein-based vaccine induced specificities distinct from those induced by wild-type measles virus or live-attenuated vaccines.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These results demonstrate the large effects of vaccination platforms on the breadth and fine-specificity of anti-measles induced humoral responses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform vaccine design by highlighting how different platforms shape antibody responses, which may impact protection against measles.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted in rhesus macaques, and the evidence strength is moderate due to the limited sample size and animal model.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the humoral response to measles virus across different vaccine platforms in rhesus macaques. Using VirScan technology, the researchers found that wild-type measles virus infection elicited broader antibody epitope reactivity compared to live-attenuated vaccines. The recombinant hemagglutinin protein-based vaccine induced distinct specificities, and all vaccinated animals expanded their antibody repertoires after challenge. The MeV-specific VarScore correlated with IgG titers, avidity, and neutralizing titers.
